name: Digital Europe Programme
evidence_rating: thin: Commission interim evaluation reports outputs and user ratings; no counterfactual or independent study of impact found
summary: Digital Europe (EUR 8.2bn, 2021-2027) funds supercomputers, AI and cybersecurity infrastructure, innovation hubs and advanced skills. The Commission's 2025 mid-term review shows outputs largely on track - the JUPITER exascale computer, over 150 innovation hubs serving 54,600 firms and 20,700 people trained - but effects on firms' productivity or digital uptake have not been measured, and no independent evaluation was found.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement contains no usable LFS indicators (1.4.4 in the extraction covers synergies); performance indicators per specific objective are set in Annex II of the Regulation, and the IA said indicators would also draw on the Digital Economy and Society Index

indicators.indicator: Joint procurements of HPC infrastructure; use of exascale systems
indicators.evidence: 19 of 30 planned procurements done; JUPITER, the EU's first exascale computer, ranked 4th on TOP500 and 1st on Green500 (its JEDI module); 19 AI Factories being deployed.

indicators.indicator: Number of European Digital Innovation Hubs and businesses served
indicators.evidence: Over 150 EDIHs covering 90% of regions by end-2024; 29,000 services to 54,600 companies; users value services at EUR 8,000-15,300 per organisation (perceived value, not measured effect).

indicators.indicator: People trained; master's programmes and courses
indicators.evidence: By end-2024: 50+ master's programmes, 530 short courses, 20,700+ people trained in AI, cybersecurity, semiconductors etc.
26 CyberHubs procured (in line with targets); network of 27 national coordination centres; first 12 cybersecurity tools deployed.

indicators.indicator: Higher EU digital capacity and uptake (e.g. SMEs highly digitised 20% in 2018)
indicators.evidence: Interim evaluation: programme on track or ahead on activities and outputs, first outcome-level benefits only now emerging; no measured effect on productivity, uptake or competitiveness.

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal establishing the Digital Europe programme (executive summary SWD(2018) 306), SWD(2018) 305
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposal establishing the Digital Europe programme (executive summary SWD(2018) 306)
literature.outcomes: digital investment gap; HPC; AI; cybersecurity; skills
literature.headline: Identifies an upstream investment gap: EU consumes one third of world HPC resources but provides about 5%; HPC investment at 60% of US level; only 20% of SMEs highly digitised; no quantified impact forecast
literature.summary_plain: The Commission said Europe was under-investing in supercomputers, AI, cybersecurity and digital skills and proposed a dedicated deployment programme, without forecasting measurable economic gains.

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Interim Evaluation of the Digital Europe Programme (Staff Working Document) and report COM(2025) 771, SWD(2025) 420; COM(2025) 771
literature.title: Interim Evaluation of the Digital Europe Programme (Staff Working Document) and report COM(2025) 771
literature.method: interim evaluation (monitoring data, surveys, perceived-value study)
literature.headline: Implementation initially delayed by late legal basis but accelerated; on track or ahead on outputs; JUPITER exascale system; 150+ EDIHs serving 54,600 companies; 20,700 people trained; 26 CyberHubs; administrative costs 4.9%; outcome-level benefits only emerging
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's mid-term review finds the EUR 8.2bn programme has delivered its planned supercomputers, innovation hubs and training places, but evidence on effects for firms or the economy is still limited to user ratings.
literature.verified: full text read (report; SWD key sections)

literature.authors: Paul Simmonds; Kleitia Zeqo; Matthias Ploeg; Alexandre Lotito; Ivette Oomens; Sophie Viscido; Emma Coroler; Jonathan Puerta; Tomas van den Broeke (Technopolis Group)
literature.title: Interim Evaluation of the Digital Europe Programme: Final report (supporting study)
literature.venue: Publications Office of the EU (study for DG CNECT), doi:10.2759/8693841
literature.method: mixed-methods programme evaluation: public consultation, surveys of beneficiaries, applicants and end users, stakeholder interviews, three case studies, monitoring-indicator analysis; plus JRC RHOMOLO model projections (ex-ante component)
literature.outcomes: progress on programme indicators, end-user reach, beneficiary-reported benefits, efficiency, coherence
literature.headline: The programme had engaged over 55,000 SMEs as end users by end-2024, which the study notes is only about 0.2% of the EU's almost 26 million SMEs; 55% of beneficiaries reported stronger cross-border networks and 36% an improved ability to deliver new products and services.
literature.summary_plain: Consultants hired by the Commission reviewed how the EU's Digital Europe funding programme performed up to 2024. It has built major infrastructure (supercomputers, AI test facilities, digital innovation hubs) and participants report benefits, but its direct reach to businesses is still small and red tape and low awareness remain problems.
literature.period_geography: EU-27 plus associated countries, 2021 to end-2024
literature.quality: Contractor study behind the Commission's SWD(2025) 420 (already listed); survey-based self-reported benefits, no counterfactual; GDP effects are model projections, not observed.
literature.interested_party: Commissioned and paid for by the European Commission (DG CNECT), which runs the programme
literature.citation: Paul Simmonds; Kleitia Zeqo; Matthias Ploeg; Alexandre Lotito; Ivette Oomens; Sophie Viscido; Emma Coroler; Jonathan Puerta; Tomas van den Broeke (Technopolis Group) (2026), Interim Evaluation of the Digital Europe Programme: Final report (supporting study), Publications Office of the EU (study for DG CNECT), doi:10.2759/8693841

literature.authors: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (Carpentier, D'Adda, Nepelski, Stake)
literature.title: European Digital Innovation Hubs Network's activities and customers: State of Play 2024 (JRC140547)
literature.method: descriptive monitoring statistics on EDIH services plus before/after comparison of Digital Maturity Assessment Tool scores for about 9,000-10,000 SMEs and 800 public organisations
literature.outcomes: services delivered, events, regional coverage, change in customers' digital maturity scores
literature.headline: By September 2024 EDIHs had organised over 5,000 events reaching more than 200,000 participants and delivered over 18,000 services; 90% of assessed users improved their digital maturity score, with AI and automation scores rising by up to 35%.
literature.summary_plain: The EU funds a network of local digital innovation hubs that help small firms and public bodies go digital. The Commission's research centre found that nine in ten organisations that were assessed twice scored higher on digital maturity after getting help.
literature.quality: Before/after scores with no control group and self-assessed tool, so gains cannot be attributed to the hubs; the Commission's own research service evaluating a Commission programme. Report PDF not accessible from here; findings read from JRC and EDIH official landing pages.
literature.interested_party: European Commission (JRC) assessing a Commission-funded network
literature.citation: European Commission, Joint Research Centre (Carpentier, D'Adda, Nepelski, Stake) (2025), European Digital Innovation Hubs Network's activities and customers: State of Play 2024 (JRC140547), JRC Science for Policy report

literature.authors: Elodie Carpentier; Diego D'Adda; Daniel Nepelski
literature.title: Which firms receive digital innovation support? Evidence from the European Digital Innovation Hubs network
literature.venue: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship
literature.method: comparison of about 15,600 EDIH customer firms with the broader European business population (firm-level demographics, performance, capital structure, innovativeness)
literature.headline: Comparing about 15,600 EDIH customer firms with the wider business population, EDIH customers are larger, faster-growing and more concentrated in high-tech, knowledge-intensive and ICT sectors, suggesting less digitally advanced firms may be systematically underserved.
literature.summary_plain: Researchers checked which companies actually use the EU-funded digital innovation hubs. They found the hubs mostly help firms that are already bigger, growing and tech-savvy, rather than the laggards the programme most wants to reach.
literature.quality: Large firm-level dataset; descriptive comparison of selection, not an impact estimate; authors are JRC staff (Commission).
literature.interested_party: Authors work at the European Commission's JRC
literature.citation: Elodie Carpentier; Diego D'Adda; Daniel Nepelski (2026), Which firms receive digital innovation support? Evidence from the European Digital Innovation Hubs network, International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship

literature.authors: Dorota Czyżewska-Misztal; Sébastien Bourdin; Fabien Nadou; Piotr Idczak
literature.title: Digital innovation hubs as territorial intermediaries: Aligning European digital strategy with local needs
literature.method: qualitative study based on 43 in-depth interviews with DIH/EDIH representatives, Commission stakeholders and network coordinators
literature.outcomes: implementation of EDIH policy at regional level, roles of hubs, policy-local mismatches
literature.headline: Based on 43 interviews, the hubs act as promoters, facilitators and enablers of SME digitalisation, but there are persistent mismatches between EU policy objectives and local implementation, especially in less digitally advanced regions.
literature.summary_plain: Interviews with people running and overseeing EU digital innovation hubs show the hubs adapt to local needs, but EU goals and what happens on the ground often do not line up, particularly in regions that are already behind digitally.
literature.quality: Qualitative interview evidence, no quantified outcomes; covers DIHs broadly, not only DEP-funded EDIHs. First names of some authors taken from Crossref record.
literature.citation: Dorota Czyżewska-Misztal; Sébastien Bourdin; Fabien Nadou; Piotr Idczak (2026), Digital innovation hubs as territorial intermediaries: Aligning European digital strategy with local needs, European Urban and Regional Studies
